#### What should I do if someone has attempted suicide?

#### Stay with them.
- Do not leave them as long as it is safe for you to do so.

 #### Call for help.
- **Call 911 or the local emergency number immediately** if there are life-threatening injuries. Or, if you think you can do so safely, take the person to the nearest hospital emergency room yourself. 
#### [Find emergency medical services near me](https://www.google.com/search?ei=ZdQ_YNiSNoj5-gSNyKGgAQ&q=find+emergency+medical+near+me&oq=find+emergency+medical+near+me&)

> You can also call a local mental health team or other suicide prevention lifelines for support. 
> - [Find an emergency mental health response team near me.](https://www.google.com/search?q=Find+an+emergency+mental+health+response+team+near+me&oq=Find+an+emergency+mental+health+response+team+near+me&aqs=chrome..69i57.344j0j7&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)
 > - [The National Suicide Prevention Hotline ](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/talk-to-someone-now/)

#### Provide lifesaving aid if needed.
- Control any major bleeding
- Support breathing 

- Try to find out if they are under the influence of alcohol or drugs or may have taken an overdose.

Tell a trusted family member or friend as soon as possible what's going on.

#### Where can I get suicide crisis support right now?

[Contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/)
 
- Call 988
Use the online [Lifeline Crisis Chat](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/chat/)
Both are free and confidential. You will be connected to a skilled, trained counselor in your area.
- The Lifeline provides 24/7, free and confidential support for people in distress, prevention and crisis resources for you or your loved ones, and best practices for professionals in the United States.

[Crisis Text Line](https://www.crisistextline.org/)
 
- Connect 24/7 to a crisis counselor by using the link above or Text HOME to 741741.
- A live, trained Crisis Counselor receives the text and responds, all from our secure online platform. The volunteer Crisis Counselor will help you move from a hot moment to a cool moment.
 
[Suicide Hotlines by State](http://www.suicide.org/suicide-hotlines.html)
- This site provides suicide hotlines by state and outside of the United States.

#### How do I ask someone if they're thinking about suicide?

**ASK**

>“Are you thinking about suicide?”

- Asking this question communicates that you're open to speaking about suicide in a non-judgmental and supportive way.
- Asking this directly can help open the door for talking about their pain and can allow everyone involved to see what next steps need to be taken.
- Other questions to ask include: 
>“How do you hurt?” and “How can I help?”

**Do not ever promise to keep their thoughts of suicide a secret.**
- Along with asking, you need to listen. 
 - Take their answers seriously and do not ignore them, especially if they indicate thoughts of suicide.
 - Listen to their reasons for being in such emotional pain. 
 - Listen for any potential reasons they want to continue to stay alive.
 - Help them focus on their reasons for living and avoid trying to impose your reasons for them to stay alive.
 - Studies show that posing this question to at-risk individuals does not increase suicides or suicidal thoughts. Acknowledging and talking about suicide tends to reduce suicide ideation.

#### How can I 'be there' for someone in suicidal crisis?

**BE THERE**

- This could be either physically present or speaking with someone on the phone and just showing support.
- Make sure you follow through with the ways in which you say you’ll be able to support the person.
 - Do not commit to anything you are not willing or able to accomplish.
 - If you are unable to be physically present with someone having thoughts of suicide, talk with them to develop some ideas for others who might be able to help (again, only others who are willing, able, and appropriate to be there).
 - Listening is also very important during this step. Find out what and who they believe will be the most effective sources of help. 
 - Being there for someone with thoughts of suicide is life-saving.
 - Increasing someone’s connectedness to others and limiting their isolation has been shown to protect against suicide.

#### How do I keep someone with suicidal thoughts safe?

**KEEP THEM SAFE**

- To establish immediate safety, it is important to know if they have already done something to try to end their life before talking with you. 
 - Does the person experiencing thoughts of suicide know how they would kill themselves?
 - Do they have a specific and detailed plan?
 - What is the timing for the plan?
 - What sort of access do they have to their planned method?
 - Knowing the answers to each of these questions can tell a lot about the immediacy and severity of danger the person is in. 
- The higher their severity of risk, the higher their capability to enact their plan might be.
- If they have immediate access to a firearm and are very serious about attempting suicide, then it may be necessary to call for emergency help or take them to the emergency department. 
- If you are unsure what to do use [The Lifeline](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/) as a resource. 
- It is important to remove any lethal means (or chosen method for a suicide attempt) to prevent suicide. 
- Keeping them safe is about showing support for them when they have thoughts of suicide by putting time and distance between the person and their chosen method.

#### How do I help a suicidal person connect to ongoing support?

**HELP THEM CONNECT**

- Helping someone with thoughts of suicide connect with ongoing supports like [Lifeline](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/) can help them establish a safety net for those moments when they find themselves in a crisis.
- Connecting them with support and resources in their communities might also be helpful.
- Help them seek out a mental health professional or other mental health resources that may be available in the community.
- Developing a safety plan can help someone know what to do when they are having thoughts of suicide.
 - A safety plan can include ways for them to identify if they start to experience significant, severe thoughts of suicide, along with what to do in those crisis moments.
 - A safety plan can also include a list of individuals to contact when a crisis occurs.

#### How do I follow up with a person after a suicide crisis?

**FOLLOW UP**

- After connecting the person with suicidal thoughts to the appropriate support systems, follow up with them to see how they are doing.
- Leave a message, send a text, or give them a call. 
- This is a good time to see if there is more that you can do to help them.
- This type of contact can continue to increase their feelings of connectedness and share your ongoing support.

#### What crisis support is available for LGBTQIA2S+ individuals?

[The Trevor Project](https://www.thetrevorproject.org/)
- Reach out to The Trevor Project for counselors if you are struggling, find answers and information, and get the tools you need to help someone else. This source is most helpful for young LGBTQIA2S+ youth and allies.

[LGBT National Senior Hotline:](https://lgbthotline.org/senior-hotline/) 888-234-7243 
- Confidential support and crisis response for LGBT elders and caretakers. (see website for hours available)

[Trans Lifeline](https://translifeline.org/hotline/): 1-877-565-8860 (United States) 
- 1-877-330-6366 (Canada)
- Confidential, crisis support for Trans people. (see website for hours available)

[American Foundation for Suicide Prevention Resources LGBTQIA2+ Crisis and Support Resources](https://afsp.org/lgbtq-crisis-and-support-resources)
- List of LGBTQ crisis hotlines and support resources if you or someone you know is experiencing mental health distress and/or is in crisis.

#### What crisis support is available for veterans?

#### [Veterans Crisis Line](https://www.veteranscrisisline.net/get-help-now/chat/?account=Veterans%20Chat) : Call: 988 and Press 1

The Veterans Crisis Line connects veterans in crisis and their families and friends with qualified, caring Department of Veterans Affairs responders through a confidential toll-free hotline, online chat, or text. 

 - [24/7 Online Chat Support](https://www.veteranscrisisline.net/get-help-now/chat/?account=Veterans%20Chat) for Veteran & Families 
 - Send a text message to 838255 to receive confidential support 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. 
- hard-of-hearing support is available

#### What should I do if I find a pet whose caretaker has died by suicide?

The pet may be trapped inside with the deceased person. Or, they may be left in a fenced yard or locked in an enclosure. In any of these cases the pet may be left without care or help.

**1. Notify police.**

**2. Touch as little as possible.**

**3. Help the pet if it is safe to do so.**

---

#### 1. Notify Police
- If you are first to the scene of the suicide, notify police. Let them know that there are animals on the premises.

#### 2. DO NOT touch the deceased caregiver or any of their belongings.
- It is not your responsibility to move or cover the body. 
- There may still be dangerous substances or items nearby.
- The police will treat the area as a crime scene.

#### 3. Help the pet. 
 IMPORTANT: Take caution while assessing the condition of the pet(s). Pets may be scared, not understand what is happening, and get protective of their pet owner and be aggressive towards others. 

**Use caution**: 
- Let the pet come to you, provide comfort to them, do not make direct eye contact. 
- **If you decide to approach**, make yourself as small as possible, get low and move slowly towards them sideways, sit or crab walk, scooting towards them sideways or crawling toward them, talk to them calmly.
- **If you cannot approach the animal safely**, wait for the police and animal control for assistance.
#### 4. If an animal’s life is at risk
- Notify police. They can tell you when it is okay to bring the pet for medical care, or, they may send the pet for care.
- Do not attempt to help the pet unless it is safe for you to do so.

#### 5. Try to stay as calm as possible. 
- For the sake of the surviving pet(s) try to keep your distress not visible to them.
- Your emotions can increase the pet’s anxiety and distress.
- You do not have to fake happiness, just try to stay calm and even toned.

#### What happens to the pet after a caretaker's suicide and can I keep it?

If the police or animal control take responsibility for the animal at the incident, there’s a high likelihood that animal will go to the shelter. Often in these situations, it can be difficult to remove the animal from the shelter due to legal protective custody. 

**You can ask for the animal to come home with you are comfortable caring for the pet, even temporarily.**

If you would like to stay connected with animal, talk to the first responders about how you can ensure the animal is being taken care of. You will need the permission of the police to take the animal.

#### How do I help someone who is suicidal and also has a pet?

#### 1. Try to communicate with the pet’s caretaker.
- Be willing to listen without judgement.
- Offer your companionship.
- Help them find psychiatric help or other mental health support.
- Provide as much assistance with this as they will allow. Remember that a suicidal person may not be able to start or complete this on their own. 

#### 2. Offer your help. 
- A person in a suicidal state may not be able to care for themselves, their home, or their pet(s). 
- Ask what you can do. 
- Offer to help clean their home or do something they are unable to. 
- If they do not feel comfortable leaving their home, offer to bring them supplies. This can include pet foods and other care items.

#### How do I help the pet of a suicidal person when I visit their home?

- Without judgement or saying anything, you can fill water bowls, feed, clean up after them, or offer other help.
- Offer to walk the dog or provide companionship to the pet(s).
- If a medical or grooming need is seen, offer to take the pet to the vet or groomer. You may need to make the appointment with their permission.

#### 4. Do not try to have the pet removed from their caretaker unless the pet’s life is in immediate danger.
- The loss of their pet(s) can potentially change someone’s suicidal thoughts to actions.
- If you feel that the pet’s life is in danger, call 911, your local animal welfare or control agency, or local Humane Society. Follow up to be sure assistance was provided. 
- If authorities are not taking action, call PETA’s 24-hour hotline at 757-622-7382. 

#### 5. If the suicidal person will not allow help or communication and they or their pet is at risk, you will need to seek assistance.
- If the person does not know you well enough, first try to contact their family or close friends if possible.
- If you do not know of anyone who can help them, call 911 and let the operator know that there are at-risk pet(s) with the person. 
- Let the operator know what type of help will be needed for the pet(s). This will prepare them to obtain the proper intervention for the pet. Do not assume that the pet will be seen and receive help if assistance is sent for the caretaker. Pets may hide with strangers in the home.

 **If you think that suicide was attempted, call 911 immediately.**
-Tell the operator what you know about the suicide attempt so help can be provided to the person.
-Let the operator know of all the pets inside and outside of the home.

#### What is suicide and what are some basic facts about it?

- **Suicide** is defined as death caused by self-directed injurious behavior with the intent to die as a result of the behavior.
- **A suicide attempt** is a non-fatal, self-directed, potentially injurious behavior with the intent to die as a result of the behavior. A suicide attempt might not result in injury.
- **Suicidal ideation** refers to thinking about, considering, or planning suicide.
 - Suicide is the **10th leading cause** of death in the United States. 

**People of any age, race, ethnicity, or sex can experience suicide risk, but certain groups have higher rates of suicide than the general U.S population.**

#### What are the risk and protective factors for suicide?

Risk Factors increase the possibility of suicide but are not always direct causes.

**Individual Risk Factors**
-	Previous suicide attempt
-	Mental illness (depression)
-	Social isolation
-	Criminal problems
-	Financial problems
-	Impulsive or aggressive tendencies
-	Job problems or loss
-	Legal problems
-	Serious illness
-	Substance use disorder

**Relationship**
-	Adverse childhood experiences such as child abuse and neglect
-	[Bullying](https://app.hazadapt.com/hazards/hate-crimes)
-	Family history of suicide
-	Relationship problems such as a break-up, violence, or loss
-	[Sexual violence](https://app.hazadapt.com/hazards/sexual-assault)

**Community**
-	Barriers to health care
-	Cultural and religious beliefs such as a belief that suicide is a noble resolution to a personal problem
-	Suicide cluster in the community

**Societal**
-	Stigma associated with mental illness or help-seeking
-	Easy access to lethal means among people at risk (firearms, medications)
-	Unsafe media portrayals of suicide

**Protective Factors**
-	Coping and problem-solving skills
-	Cultural and religious beliefs that discourage suicide
-	Connections to friends, family, and community support
-	Supportive relationships with care providers
-	Availability of physical and mental health care
-	Limited access to lethal means among people at risk

#### What are the warning signs that someone may be suicidal?

[The warning signs for suicide can include:](https://medlineplus.gov/suicide.html)

- Talking about wanting to die or wanting to kill oneself
- Making a plan or looking for a way to kill oneself, such as searching online
- Buying a gun or stockpiling pills
- Feeling empty, hopeless, trapped, or like there is no reason to live
- Being in unbearable pain
- Talking about being a burden to others
- Using more alcohol or drugs 
- Acting anxious or agitated, behaving recklessly
- Sleeping too little or too much
- Withdrawing from family or friends or feeling isolated
- Showing rage or talking about seeking revenge
- Displaying extreme mood swings
- Saying goodbye to loved ones, putting affairs in order
- Some people may tell others about their suicidal thoughts. But others may try to hide them. This can make some of the signs harder to spot.

#### What is self-harm and why do people do it?

[**What is Self-Harm?**](https://www.nami.org/About-Mental-Illness/Common-with-Mental-Illness/Self-harm)

*Self-harm or self-injury means hurting yourself on purpose.*
-	Common methods include
 - Cutting with a sharp object
 - Burning oneself
 - Pulling out hair
 - Picking at wounds
 - Extreme injuries can result in broken bones. 
-	Hurting yourself or thinking about it is a sign of emotional distress.
 - Emotions will grow more intense with continued use of self-harm as a coping mechanism.
 - It is important to learn other ways to tolerate mental pain for long-term wellness.
-	Self-harm also causes feelings of shame
 - The scars that are left behind from frequent cutting or burning can be permanent. 
 - Drinking or doing drugs can increase the risk of causing a more severe injury.
 - Self-harm can also negatively affect work and relationships due to people wanting to avoid certain situations so that people won’t see their scars. 

**Why Do People Self-Harm?**

*Self-harm is not a mental illness, it is a behavior that means there is a need for someone to learn better coping skills.*
-	Self-harm is most common during the teenage and young adult years. 
-	People who have experienced trauma, neglect, or abuse are at higher risk of self-harm. 
-	The urge to hurt yourself may start with overwhelming anger, frustration, or pain.
-	Self-harm can feel like a release when someone is not sure how to deal with their emotions. 
-	Sometimes, injuring yourself stimulates the body’s endorphins or pain-killing hormones, which can raise your mood.
-	If someone doesn’t feel many emotions, hurting themselves allows them to feel something instead of nothing. 
-	The shame and guilt that form after self-harm can cause someone to hurt themselves again, creating a vicious circle. 
-	Self-harm is not the same as attempting suicide. 
 - It is a symptom of emotional pain that does need to be taken seriously. 
 - Self-harm can mean that there is an increased risk of feeling suicidal.
 - It is important to find treatment for the underlying emotions.

#### What treatments help with self-harm?

**Treatment and Coping**

*Effective treatments for self-harm that allow a person to feel in control again do exist.*
-	Psychotherapy can be very helpful for a person to learn new coping mechanisms. 
-	The first step to getting help is to talk to someone you trust (adult, friend, or medical professional), ideally a psychiatrist. 
-	The more information you can give to a psychiatrist the better your treatment plan will be. 
-	In certain circumstances medications can be prescribed.

#### What do I do if I think someone is thinking about suicide?

*If you are worried about someone you know who may be hurting themselves, ask them how they are doing and be prepared to listen to the answer, even if it makes you uncomfortable.*
-	It is important to tell them that you are there to help even if you do not fully understand.
-	Do not dismiss their emotions or try to turn it into a joke. 
-	Encourage them to get treatment by letting them know self-harm is not uncommon and there are doctors and therapists that can help. 
-	You can also offer to help find treatment. 

**If a friend or loved one talks or behaves in a way that makes you believe they might attempt suicide, do not try to handle the situation alone:**
 - Get help from a trained professional as quickly as possible. The person may need to be hospitalized until the suicidal crisis has passed.
 - Encourage the person to call a suicide hotline number. 
 - In the U.S., call or text 988 the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (previously the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline) to reach a trained counselor. Use that same number and press "1" to reach the Veterans Crisis Line.

[What to do if you believe someone may be thinking about suicide](https://web.archive.org/web/20210515190037/https://store.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/SAMHSA_Digital_Download/PEP20-01-03-001.pdf)

**If there is no immediate danger**
 -	Ask them if they are thinking about killing themselves (This will not put the idea into their head or make it more likely that they will attempt suicide).
 -	Listen without judging and show you care.
 -	Stay with the person (or make sure the person is in a private, secure place with another caring person) until you can get further help.
 -	Remove any objects that could be used in a suicide attempt.
 -	Call or text the [988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline](https://988lifeline.org/) and follow their guidance.

#### What suicide prevention resources are available?

[How Can You Help Yourself?](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/help-yourself/) 
There are wonderful people who care about you and are here to help you get through this crisis.
- They can help you get connected to mental health support, a therapist, or support group and making a safety plan. 
 
[Help Someone Else](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/help-someone-else/)
 If someone you know is struggling emotionally or having a hard time, you can be the difference in getting them the help they need. 
- It is important to take care of yourself when you are supporting someone through a difficult time, as this may stir up difficult emotions. If it does, please reach out to mental health support.

[Be The One to Help Save a Life](https://www.bethe1to.com/?_ga=2.3703988.586201591.1644444836-858996413.1644444836)
- The Lifeline network and its partners are working to change the conversation surrounding suicide and take action that promotes healing, help, and gives hope. Together, we can prevent suicide by learning to help ourselves, help others, seek consultation from trained providers (hotlines and clinicians), and seek hospital care when necessary. 

[Suicide Prevention Resource Center](https://www.sprc.org/)
- The SPRC advances suicide prevention through collaborations within the community, educational resources and outreach programs. It is devoted entirely to advancing the implementation of the National Strategy for Suicide Prevention.

[Take 5 to Save Lives](https://www.take5tosavelives.org/)
- By taking 5 minutes to get involved and become informed, you will be part of a worldwide movement to save lives. Learn the warning signs, know how to help, practice self-care, reach out, and spread the word. 

[National Action Alliance For Suicide Prevention](https://theactionalliance.org/)
- The National Action Alliance for Suicide Prevention (Action Alliance) works with more than 250 national partners to advance the National Strategy for Suicide Prevention.

#### Why is self-care important for suicide prevention?

**What is Self-Care?**
Self-care involves activities that help with physical and mental fitness and is a very important part of overall health.

**Self-care is important for everyone.**
It is an essential part of building resilience and helps us cope with stressful situations in our lives.

#### How do I practice good emotional hygiene for mental health?

Similar to taking showers and brushing our teeth for personal hygiene, we need to take care of our mental health.
 
**1. Address emotional pain:** Feelings of grief, anger, rejection, or failure.
 - Be aware of what causes your emotional pain.
 - Letting emotional pain last too long can lead to depression and other mental health conditions. 
- Identify troubling conditions or situations.
 - Examples may include:
 - Work or school presentation 
 - A crisis at work or home 
 - A challenge with someone you are close with
 - A dramatic change such as loss of a job

 **2. [Maintain your self-esteem](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/adult-health/in-depth/self-esteem/art-20045374).**

*Self-esteem is the level of confidence you have in yourself to accomplish your goals and is very important for mental wellbeing.*
 - Self-esteem is how you view your self-worth and can affect how you respond to different situations.
 - Feelings of failure or rejection can lower self-esteem. 
 - Have self-compassion.
 - Use hopeful statements.
> "Even though it is tough, I can handle this situation." 
 
 - Forgive yourself, everyone makes mistakes. 
- Focus on the positive.
- Encourage yourself.

 **3. Avoid repetitive negative thoughts.**
 
Try to disrupt negative thoughts with positive ones by finding a positive distraction.

 - Do something that requires concentration to help prevent negative thinking. 
 
- Too much negative thinking can lead to depression. 
- Convert negative thoughts into positive ones.
> From: " I will never be good at math." 

> To: " I will work harder to get better at math."

**4. Make time for family, friends, and community.**

Feeling connected can help prevent depression. Feeling lonely and disconnected is bad for mental health.

 - Make time to connect with friends or family regularly even if just for a phone call or FaceTime. 
- Connecting with your community or others that have shared similar experiences can be a source of support.
 - Going to social activities such as book clubs or exercise classes can also have a positive effect on your mental health.

#### What physical self-care helps prevent suicide?

#### PHYSICAL SELF-CARE
 **Nourish your body with healthy food.**
 
 Healthy foods are not only good for your physical health but can also improve your mood. 
 - To increase your energy and overall wellness you should:
 - Eat plenty of whole foods- fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
 - Get nutritious sources of protein
 - Limit the amount of sugar, salt, saturated fat, and trans fats you consume. These are abundant in processed foods. 
 - Caffeine and alcohol can worsen or trigger anxiety. It’s best to drink water to stay clear, focused, and hydrated!

**Get enough sleep**

Lack of sleep due to stress or other issues can lead to serious health problems. Doctors recommend seven to nine hours of sleep each night. 
 
Some tips to get enough sleep include:
 - Stick to the same bedtime most nights. 
 - No screens (computer, TV, phone) at least one hour before bed.
 - Try to destress before bed. Perhaps meditate, stretch, listen to soothing music, take a hot shower or bath. Find what helps you relax. 
 - Exercise earlier in the day can help you rest easier at night. 

**Move your body.**
 - It is recommended that you get your body moving and keep your heart rate elevated for at least 150 minutes per week or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise per week. 
 - Exercise also helps you increase your energy, improve your mood, and fall asleep.
 - Consult a doctor if you are new to exercise or have health issues. 

**Help others**
Helping others can also help you. Volunteer at a local food bank or soup kitchen, offer help to a family or friend in need, or donate to a charity. 

**Manage your stress**
Stress is your body’s response to the mental and physical demands of life. Common stressors include daily responsibilities such as work, school, and family. More severe stressors come from traumatic events, the loss of a loved one, illness, or some other life-altering event. 

It is important to take steps to manage stress to avoid long term effects of stress. These steps include:
 1. Identifying your stressors: write a list separating out stressors you can and cannot control.
 2. Try to find solutions for stressors that you can control.
 3. For the stressors that you cannot control, find ways to control how you **react** to them. 
 4. Listening to music can improve mood and help you destress.
 5. Therapists are also a great resource to help you manage stress. 

**Manage other medical or physical problems**
 - Pay attention to your body.
 - Mental and physical health are connected to each other. 
 - It is important to deal with any health issues you might have. 
 - Do not be afraid to ask for help whether it is from family, friends or a medical provider.
 - Everyone can help you in some way.

#### What suicide prevention trainings can I take?

**[Applied Suicide Intervention Skills Training (ASIST)](https://www.livingworks.net/asist)**

- ASIST is a 2-day training program that teaches participants how to assist those at risk for Suicidal Thinking, Behavior, and Attempts. Although many healthcare professionals use ASIST, anyone 16 years or older can use the approach, regardless of professional background. ASIST workshops cost money to attend, with costs varying by training site.

**[Question. Persuade. Refer. (QPR)](https://qprinstitute.com/)**

- QPR refers to three steps that anyone can learn to help prevent suicide. The QPR's mission is to reduce suicidal behaviors and save lives by providing innovative, practical, and proven suicide prevention training. The signs of crisis are all around us. They believe that quality education empowers all people, regardless of their background, to make a positive difference in the life of someone they know.

#### What are the goals of suicide prevention support?

Everyone has a role to play to save lives and create healthy and strong individuals, families, and communities. 

Knowing the risk factors, recognizing the warning signs, and seeking support can help prevent suicide. 

#### Goals Supporting Suicide Prevention
- Reduce factors that increase the risk for suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
- Increase the factors that help strengthen, support, and protect individuals from suicide. 
- Having access to health care can decrease suicidal thoughts and behaviors. 
- Staying connected to family and community support.
 - [The Suicide Prevention Hotline](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/) 800-273-8255 

**When the Mental Health Crisis Involves the Risk of Suicide**

The risk of suicide is a major concern for people with mental health conditions and those who love them. Encouraging someone to get help is the first step towards safety. 

People who attempt suicide typically feel overwhelming emotional pain, frustration, loneliness, hopelessness, powerlessness, worthlessness, shame, guilt, rage, and/or self-hatred. Social isolation is common in the lives of those with mental illness can reinforce the belief that no one cares if they live or die.

**Any talk of suicide should always be taken seriously.** Most people who attempt suicide have
given some warning—but this is not always the case.

#### What suicide prevention support is available for Indigenous communities?

[Suicide Prevention Lifeline](https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/help-yourself/native-americans/)
- Depression and suicide affect people of all ages and populations, but Native American and Alaskan Native populations can be at a higher risk due to historical trauma, adverse childhood experiences, and lack of connection to necessary resources. If you’re struggling, the Lifeline is available to help, 24/7.

[Suicide Prevention in Indigenous Communities](https://www.nami.org/Your-Journey/Identity-and-Cultural-Dimensions/Indigenous/Suicide-Prevention-in-Indigenous-Communities)
- Provides information on what increases the risk of suicide and how communities can take action to prevent suicide in indigenous communities.

#### What suicide prevention resources are available for veterans?

[Veteran Suicide Prevention](https://www.va.gov/health-care/health-needs-conditions/mental-health/suicide-prevention/)
- If you are a veteran in a mental health crisis and you are thinking about hurting yourself—or you know a veteran who is considering this—get help right away. You are not alone.
 
[National Action Alliance for Suicide Prevention](https://theactionalliance.org/veteran-and-military-suicide-prevention-resources)
- This site provides more veteran and military suicide prevention resources.

#### As a teen, what should I do if I'm worried a friend is suicidal?

*It may be hard to tell whether a friend or classmate is suicidal, and you may be afraid of taking action and being wrong. If someone's behavior or talk makes you think he or she might be suicidal, the person may be struggling with some major issues, even if not considering suicide at the moment. You can help the person get to the right resources and know they are not alone.*

1. Ask the person directly about their feelings, even though it may be awkward. 
2. Listen and take it seriously. 
 - Just talking to someone who really cares can make a big difference.

#### As a teen, what should I do if I'm worried a friend or classmate may be suicidal?

*It may be hard to tell whether a friend or classmate is suicidal, and you may be afraid of taking action and being wrong. If someone's behavior or talk makes you think he or she might be suicidal, the person may be struggling with some major issues, even if not considering suicide at the moment. You can help the person get to the right resources and know they are not alone.*

1. Ask the person directly about their feelings, even though it may be awkward. 
2. Listen and take it seriously. 
 - Just talking to someone who really cares can make a big difference.
3. If you're still concerned after talking with them, share your concerns with a trusted, responsible adult, like a teacher or guidance counselor.

#### How can I keep a pet safe when its owner is suicidal?

People who are experiencing deep depression, trauma, or other mental illnesses that have led to suicidal thoughts or plans often struggle to care for themselves. This can make caring for another being like a pet difficult or impossible. Remember that the neglect is not intentional. 

**Neglect May Look Like:**
- forgetting to provide food and water
- not caring for the pet’s medical or other needs

#### Help Both the Person and the Pets
In many cases, the key to helping a pet whose caretaker is suicidal is to try to help the person at the same time. Sometimes, helping someone through a difficult time can look like helping lift some of the chores that comes with caring for pets.

Prepare for the possibility that the suicidal person may not accept help or even be willing to communicate.

**Keep in mind that having the pet removed from a suicidal person may be damaging.**
 
- The pet may be their only support system. 
- The pet may be what is keeping them from acting on suicidal thoughts.

#### What should I expect emotionally after a suicide attempt?

#### What to Expect While Recovering from a Suicide Attempt

**Emotions**
- Exhaustion
- Extreme fatigue
- Anger
- Embarrassment or shame
- Overwhelmed

*This is most likely the hardest day of your life, whether you attempted suicide or seriously thought about it. All of the emotions you are feeling are valid and to be expected. Things can and will get better.*

#### What should I do after leaving the emergency department after a suicide attempt?

**What to do after the Emergency Department**
- Schedule an appointment with a mental health provider.
 - The hospital can provide information about following up with treatment.
- Understand and review your prescribed treatments with your doctors. 
- It may be necessary for you to stay in the hospital. If this is the case, discuss your next steps with the hospital.
- Hospital staff or a social worker should help you with this. 

#### Plans For Follow-Up Care
You and, if appropriate, a family member should work closely with a therapist at the hospital to make sure the plan is meaningful and effective. 
- Make sure you understand and are comfortable with the plan.
 - If the emergency medical professionals feel that you need more care than they can offer, you may be referred for inpatient hospitalization.

#### What if I don't want to go to the hospital after a suicide attempt?

People generally have the right to consent to or refuse treatment. However, if the emergency physician believes you are a danger to yourself or others, they are required to keep you and others safe. You may be hospitalized involuntarily for a limited period of time.
Laws about involuntary hospitalization vary by state.

#### How can I work on long-term recovery after a suicide attempt?

**Be kind to yourself**
- You have just survived a life-threatening health crisis and you deserve to take the time you need to recover.
- You may not understand all of your thoughts and feelings but that is okay.
- It is okay to not have all of the answers right now.

**Take care of your health**
- Exercising, eating right, getting enough sleep, and spending time with healthy people can have a huge impact on your health and mood.

**Find a mental health professional**
- A good therapist or doctor can help you put this experience in proper perspective. They can also help you develop a safety plan and find ways to address life stressors.

**Understand how to navigate your health insurance**
- After surviving a life-threatening health crisis, deciphering health insurance bills can be overwhelming. The National Alliance on Mental Health (NAMI) has created a guide to help.

**Try a support group**
- There are different kinds of support groups, including those for depression and other mental health conditions and for those who have survived a suicide attempt. A group can help you know you are not alone.

**Talk to those you trust**
- When you’re ready, let them know what happened and that you want them to help you stay safe.

**Have a safety plan**
- Recognize what puts you at risk.
- Find coping strategies that do not rely on the presence of others.
- Engage with people and go to places that help take your mind off your problems.
- Reach out to family or friends that can help you in a crisis.
- Call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-8255.
- Keep your environment safe.

#### How can I support someone recovering from a suicide attempt?

**Prepare Yourself**
- Prepare to be there and stay involved, offer support, and listen without judgment. Accept that this is not something you can fix. 
- Prepare to have difficult conversations with them and learn about how they are feeling. 

**Help them create a safety plan**
 - The safety plan will help them and whoever else might be supporting them to know what to do if they become suicidal again. 

**Talk to them** 
 - It is okay to talk about suicide, emotions, or anything else they might want to talk about. 
- Try to keep in contact with them even if they ignore you. 
- If they don't want to talk to you, ask others that you both trust to support them.

**Seek professional help**
- Let them know about free counseling services and connect them to a counselor or doctor.
- You could also offer to go with them or help them set up an appointment.
- Don't forget to set up an appointment for yourself if you need to. 

**Be Positive**
- Identify positive things in their life to help them feel hope that things will get better. 
- Support them by doing things that they enjoy and staying physically active and connecting with others. 
- Help them identify things in their life that they can change to feel better.
 - This could mean cutting back on alcohol or drugs, increasing exercise, sleeping, and making time for themselves. 
- Let them know you care and accept them for who they are. 
- When they are ready you can support them in making future plans and goals. 

**Self-care**
- Remember to take care of yourself when caring for others.
- See the Practicing Self-Care section.

**Build a support network**
- Include others to help you and the person you are supporting.
- Ask the person you are helping what they need and who they want to be involved with.
- They need at least 3-5 people to support them.
- Gather the support group in a safe space.
- Talk openly and honestly about the situation.
- Talk to the person you’re supporting about what they will do if they feel suicidal again, how they plan to keep safe, and how others can help with this.
- Develop a plan together to support the person and identify how different people can help. 
 - Get professional help if you need it. Talk to your local doctor, medical center, community mental health team, or counseling service.

#### Is it okay to ask someone why they attempted suicide?

**Asking 'why'**
- It is okay to ask someone why they attempted suicide.
- It is also important to know that they may not know why.
- Some of the reasons people have given for attempting suicide have included:
 - The situation was so unbearable, I couldn’t think of an alternative.
 - I felt trapped. There was no other way I could get away.
 - I was just so agitated and completely on the edge all the time, I needed to do something.
 - I felt overwhelmed and out of control.
 - I needed to get help and let others know how desperate I felt.
 - I felt like a failure and a burden. I just wanted to make it easier for those around me.
 - I don’t know why I did it.

**What not to do:**
- Do not use words like "unsuccessful" or "failed" when talking about a suicide attempt.
- Just use words like "suicide attempt" or "attempted to take their own life."
- Don't ask about how they harmed themselves unless it is necessary for you to know to keep them safe.
- If you are not a part of their core support network you do not need to know what method they used.
- Don't make them feel guilty or blamed (don't say "how could you do this to me?)."
- Don't give up on them.

#### How do I cope with losing someone to suicide?

#### If you know someone who has attempted or completed suicide, you may experience many confusing and painful emotions. 

**Some possible effects after losing someone to suicide include:** 

- Serious emotional and physical impacts 
- Impaired health and sense of well-being 
- Feelings of shock, anger, guilt, depression, anxiety
- Some who have lost loved ones may even experience suicidal thoughts themselves.

**Actions you can take to help yourself recover from loss:**

- Find a support group. You do not have to go through the grieving process alone. 

- Do not feel pressured to discuss what happened right away. Do what feels right for you, and get support from family and friends when you feel like talking about it. 

- Writing about your feelings, or writing a letter to your loved one, may be helpful to deal with your emotions. 

- Ask for help. Get support from counselors, therapists, family, and friends. 

- If you are having thoughts of suicide, seek immediate help. See Suicide Crisis Support Resources for ways that you can get help. 

**How to support others who have lost someone to suicide:** 

- Accept their feelings and provide support with empathy. Do not judge how they may be feeling. 

- Check in on them during holidays, birthdays, and anniversaries. These events may bring up painful memories of the lost loved one. 

- Do not avoid talking about the person who died by suicide. Use the name of the person when talking to survivors. This helps remove stigma from the suicide, and helps to remember the loved one in other ways. 

- Ask if they are having thoughts of suicide themselves. Get them help if you see [warning signs](https://medlineplus.gov/suicide.html). 

- [What to do if you believe someone may be thinking about suicide](https://store.samhsa.gov/product/helping-your-loved-one-suicidal-guide-family-friends/PEP20-01-03-001).

#### What is suicide contagion and how can it be prevented?

**What is suicide contagion?**
- An increase in suicide attempts and suicides. 
- Occurs after hearing or reading about suicides in the media, in print, or online. 
- Suicides of popular celebrities can lead to a rise in other suicides. 
- Can also occur after the suicide of a friend, family member, classmate, or community member. 

**Who is affected by suicide contagion?**
- Anyone can be affected, but people who are already struggling or may be thinking about suicide can be most affected. 
- Teens are often most vulnerable. 
- People with mental health conditions, disabilities, and/or poor social support may also be more vulnerable. 

**How can suicide contagion be prevented?**
- How the media reports on suicides plays a large role. 
- Media outlets should not release detailed information about suicides, like the methods used. 
- Reporting on suicide should focus on informing, not overemphasizing.
- The main message should be to get help if needed. 

**What can be done about suicide contagion?**
- Provide mental health resources for those who are struggling. See Suicide Crisis and Suicide Prevention Support sections for specific assistance. 
- Focus on stories about people who have struggled and pulled through. 
- Avoid glamorizing or overexaggerating suicide, particularly if a famous person has died. 
- Avoid sharing details about the suicide.
- Do not oversimplify the reason for a suicide - this can cause others to think it is a viable solution to a problem. 
- Do not stigmatize emotional pain - encourage discussion and seeking help. 

*Choose words carefully:* 
- Do not call suicide “successful,” “unsuccessful” or a “failed attempt.” 
- Do not say “committed suicide" or "completed suicide.” Instead, use “died by suicide,” “killed him/her/theirself,” or “ended his/her/their life.”
- Do not describe suicide as “inexplicable” or “without warning."
- Do not avoid the subject but be ready to discuss it thoughtfully. 

**Following exposure to suicide or suicidal behaviors, decrease suicide risk by having family members, friends, peers, and colleagues of the victim evaluated by a mental health professional.**

#### How do pets grieve after losing their human caretaker?

#### What to Expect
Pets will grieve the loss of their caretaker similar to humans experiencing loss. Be patient with them and give them time to adjust to the changes. 

#### Pets may show their grief with behavioral changes:

- Hiding
- Avoidance of triggers
- Refusing to repeat any events similar to those that led to the traumatic event (ex.car rides, leashed walks, etc.) 
- Freezing
- Restlessness
- Pacing
- Destruction of surroundings
- Aggression
- Anxiety
- Depression
- Avoidance of people

#### Pets may also develop medical issues:

- Excessive paw-licking or chewing
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Anorexia
- Panting 
- Accidents inside the house
- Twitching when sleeping.

#### How do I support a pet that is grieving their human?

You may see them wait by the door and watch for their previous pet owner. It is ok that animals feel sadness and they appreciate you providing positive distraction and love. You can be there for them by being a new source of happiness.

#### Supporting Pets in Grief
- Pheromone sprays, diffusers or treated items (dog and cat specific) to reduce anxiety.
- Make an effort to maintain familiar routines, items, food, and treats.
- Try to stay upbeat, even when the pet is grieving. 

- Gently distract with positive activity

- Avoid unintentionally reinforcing and encouraging “waiting for them” or if you see them being sad and grieving. Try distracting the a-animal from the sad state by first responding with positive activities. Give treats and physical affection, 
- Think about focusing on your bond with the surviving pet. Think about what makes them happy, and do more than that. For some dogs, this might be getting lots of attention, and for others, it might be training, play or longer walks. Human or animal, loss affects us all but we cope best when we care for each other.

#### How do I keep familiar routines for a grieving pet?

**Outside time:** Routines with familiar walking places and times of walks
 
**Food & Feeding**
- If you are unsure, you can ask the pet’s vet, or start with a bland diet, then slowly transition to the intended long-term diet.
- BLAND FOOD example: Plain Boiled chicken, plain boiled white rice, DO NOT add oil or spices. 
- Use the animals own familiar bowl or trough
- Using the pet’s own bed, bowls, and supplies. Reducing change helps them find stability and cope with the bigger change of losing their human.

**Try to do things that make them happy and feel cared for**
- Being with them and talking to them
- Walks
- Play time
- Treats
- Going for a ride in the car
- Making sure they have a comfortable safe place in your home

#### What veterinary support is available for grieving pets?

- If the pet is experiencing medical changes or significant behavioral changes, they will need to see a veterinarian right away.
- If the pet’s behavioral changes are causing a poor quality of life, they are showing aggression, or unusual or troubling behaviors a veterinary behaviorist may be needed. Your regular veterinarian can usually recommend a provider in your area. 

**Veterinary behaviorists** are veterinary doctors who specialize in pet behavior. They can prescribe medications and provide behavior modification tools that most regular vets cannot. 

- National directory of veterinary behaviorists: [American College of Veterinary Behaviorists](https://www.dacvb.org/search/advanced.asp)

- [Find an American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior provider near you.](https://avsab.org/directory/)

#### How do I find a new safe home for a pet whose owner died by suicide?

**You can help ensure the pet finds a loving, safe home**

If possible, it can be helpful to have the rescued pet stay with a familiar person while they are recovering. This may be family or a friend of the caretaker. Ideally, it is someone the pet already knows. 

- If this is a good home, try to keep the pet with the familiar person for life.
- If there is not someone who can care for the pet, help to advocate for the pet’s wellbeing.
- Contact rescue groups and let them know all you can about the pet. This can help the pet find the right adopter. 

If you are trying to find out what happened to the pet after the suicide, ask the police or responder for the animal ID or look for the animal in local shelters if that is not an option.
